metadata.title: From Tregs to tissue remodelling: FOXP3 and IL-35 in the inflammatory landscape of nasal polyps

sections.text: Objective Inflammatory nasal polyps (NPs) are a chronic condition of the nasal mucosa linked with prolonged airway obstruction, frequent infections, and immune dysregulation. While the exact mechanisms underlying NP development remain unknown, new research indicates that immune-regulatory pathways are essential. Forkhead box P3 (FOXP3) and Interleukin-35 (IL-35) have attracted much interest. Methods In this narrative review, we examine how regulatory T cells (Tregs) release the potent immunosuppressive cytokine IL-35, suppressing effector T cell responses and encouraging Treg proliferation. Studies have shown that IL-35 is essential for preserving immunological homeostasis. FOXP3, a crucial transcription factor necessary for the development and maintenance of developing and maintaining immunological tolerance, controls the development and activity of Tregs. The pathophysiology of NPs is also included in this review, along with pertinent immunological indicators linked to the advancement of the condition. Result The balance between inflammatory and regulatory responses is upset in NP patients due to dysregulation of IL-35 and FOXP3, exacerbating chronic inflammation. Studying how they interact offers novel insight into the pathophysiology of NP and identifies potential curative approaches, such as Treg regulation and IL-35 supplementation. Parallel to this, pharmacological treatments such as corticosteroids and biologics (such as dupilumab) aim to reduce type 2 inflammation. Conclusion FOXP3 and IL-35 play an important role in maintaining immunological homeostasis, and their dysregulation is associated with the persistent inflammation seen in NPs. Relying on these regulatory mechanisms may represent a promising therapeutic direction, although further experimental and clinical validation is required beyond existing anti-inflammatory therapies. Further investigation is necessary to confirm their clinical relevance.

Nasal polyps (NPs) are edematous, noncancerous growths originating from the nasal cavity and paranasal sinus mucosa. They are frequently linked to chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS). These growths lower the quality of life by producing symptoms such as nasal blockage, anosmia (loss of smell), rhinorrhea, and facial pain [ 1 ]. Based on inflammatory endotypes, NPs are classified into two types: eosinophilic nasal polyps (ENPs), which are primarily linked to type 2 (Th2) inflammation and often associated with conditions like asthma and aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD), and neutrophil nasal polyps (NNPs), which are related to non-type 2 inflammations and are frequently associated with bacterial invasion or environmental harmful factors [ 2 ]. NPs have multiple network pathogeneses, including immunological dysfunction, environmental irritants, and genetic disorders. Their development pointed mainly to chronic inflammation, with innate and adaptive immune dysregulation being a regulatory factor. Among the early stages of polyp formation, one is epithelial barrier failure, which allows allergens, infections, and pollutants to enter the mucosa. Therefore, epithelial-derived cytokines such as thymic stromal lymphopoietin (TSLP), IL-25, and IL-33 are secreted due to this disruption, intensifying type 2 inflammatory responses [ 3 ]. Innate immune cells, such as eosinophils and mast cells, are also significantly involved in causing inflammation. Eosinophils aid in tissue remodelling and oedema in ENPs, while mast cells release histamine and other proinflammatory mediators. However, neutrophilic infiltration, which produces reactive oxygen species and tissue-damaging proteases, is a characteristic of NNPs [ 4 , 5 ]. Adaptive immune dysregulation further inflames NP pathogenesis. Th2 cells predominate in ENPs and release IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13 cytokines. These cytokines influence processes such as eosinophil recruitment (IL-5), IgE synthesis (IL-4 and IL-13), and mucus hypersecretion [ 6 ]. Tregs are significant contributors to immunological homeostasis and are characterized by FOXP3 expression. However, both the number and suppressive function of Tregs are often flawed in NP tissues, contributing to chronic inflammation [ 7 ]. Moreover, dysregulated cytokine networks involving TNF-α, IL-6, and chemokines such as eotaxin further increase immune cell recruitment and inflammatory responses [ 8 ]. While IL-17 promotes neutrophilic inflammation in NNPs, IL-5 is a key cytokine in eosinophilic inflammation, encouraging eosinophil activation and survival [ 7 ]. Given significant advances in understanding the inflammatory mechanisms associated with NPs, the current investigation has primarily focused on pro-inflammatory pathways, with minimal emphasis on immunoregulatory systems. The functions of FOXP3⁺ Tregs and immunosuppressive cytokines, such as IL-35, in regulating NP inflammation are inadequately described. Recent data indicate that IL-35 may be pivotal in limiting excessive immunological responses and augmenting Treg function; however, the findings are disparate and need complete integration. The interaction of FOXP3 expression, IL-35 signalling, and tissue remodelling in NPs has not been thoroughly assessed. Therefore, there is a clear need for a focused, integrative review that unifies current knowledge of FOXP3 and IL-35 in NP pathogenesis. This review aims to (i) critically assess the roles of FOXP3⁺ Tregs and IL-35 in regulating inflammatory responses in NPs, (ii) explore their benefaction to tissue remodelling and disease heterogeneity, and (iii) determine existing knowledge gaps and future research endeavours, especially in relation to their future potential as therapeutic targets. This review aims to enhance understanding of immunoregulatory mechanisms in NPs and to facilitate the formulation of targeted therapeutic strategies.

Th2 cells and group 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2), which generate type 2 cytokines such as IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13, together with other inflammatory mediators, are the main drivers of type 2 inflammation [ 8 – 12 ]. These cells and cytokines are recognised as biomarkers in the circulating blood and nasal cavity tissues of CRS patients, and they play a significant role in the pathological process of both inflammation and remodelling in CRS [ 13 ]. In the pathophysiology of type 2 inflammatory airway disorders, type 2 cytokines play various roles. The differentiation, maturation, mobilisation, and survival of IL-5Rα + eosinophil progenitors in the bone marrow are all significantly influenced by IL-5 [ 14 ]. Furthermore, IL-5 promotes the growth of additional type 2 cells, such as basophils and mast cells [ 15 ], and IL-4 and IL-13 contribute to B-cell class switching and IgE production, which in turn, cause tissue remodelling, barrier disruption, and the degranulation of mast cells and basophils, releasing proinflammatory mediators [ 16 , 17 ]. The IL-4R/signal transduction and activator of transcription 6 (STAT6) signalling pathway is shared by the two associated cytokines IL-4 and IL-13, which mediate their activities [ 17 ]. In addition to smooth muscle hyperplasia and contractility, IL-13 is implicated in mucus formation and goblet-cell hyperplasia [ 16 , 17 ]. Furthermore, the development of mucus plugs due to mucus production is similarly linked to IL-13-mediated negative effects on the layers of epithelial barriers [ 18 ]. Previous studies have also suggested that IL-4 might be responsible for IL-13 pro-fibrotic effects [ 14 ]. Nevertheless, it has been discovered that IL-13 can cause fibrosis even when the conventional IL-4R or STAT6-mediated signalling route is inhibited; IL-13 can cause fibrosis by triggering other signalling pathways via its receptors [ 19 ].

sections.section: Effect Of Cytokines On Remodelling And Immune Dysregulation
sections.text: Primarily, consider that TGF-β (TGF-β refers to TGF-β1), fibroblast growth factors (FGF), and VEGF have been found to have an intense influence on the pathological process of CRS inflammation via previous studies. Among these, TGF-β1 (fibrogenic factor) is more predominant, up to 80%, and is a copious member of the TGF family [ 20 ]. It has been suggested that variations in TGF-β levels between CRS with NPs(CRSwNP) and CRS without NPs (CRSsNP) may be a contributing factor to the distinct remodelling properties of CRS tissue remodelling [ 21 ]. Meanwhile, TGF-β1 has two functions in the inflammatory immunological effects in CRS. TGF β 1 can both develop inflammation by inducing differentiation of T lymphocytes into inflammatory Th17 cells [ 22 ] and repress the production of different inflammatory cytokines and mediators, such as IL-1, IL-8, and TNF-α [ 23 ], which in turn suppresses the secretion of mediators from eosinophils and increases their rate of apoptosis [ 24 ]. By having a variety of anti-inflammatory actions, it can also strongly suppress the growth and cytokine production of Th1 and Th2 clones, as well as naive T cells [ 25 ], and encourage the development of T regulatory cells [ 26 ]. In nasal polyposis, IL-13-induced airway epithelial remodelling results in the growth of tuft and goblet cells and the loss of ciliated cells. Increased prostaglandin activity in the epithelium, where these compositional alterations occur, probably adds to the altered tissue function. It is possible that PGE2 (Prostaglandin 2)-induced tissue effects and IL-13-driven epithelium remodelling work together to cause the sinus opacification seen on radiography [ 27 ]. It is well known that during type 2 inflammation, IL-13 plays a crucial role in promoting goblet cell development. Recent research using single-cell sequencing of epithelial cells has shown a correlation between the clinical severity of nasal polyposis and IL-13-driven epithelial remodelling [ 27 ]. It is well known that anomalies in innate and adaptive immune responses, mainly driven by IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13, lead to pathological type 2 inflammation [ 28 ]. Together with IL-5, eotaxin is another important maintaining component in airway inflammation [ 29 ]. Their synergistic effects render eosinophils more responsive to chemokines. Age-group-specific cytokine involvement in illness progression may exhibit different patterns [ 30 ].

A transcription factor called FOXP3 is necessary for the growth and operation of Tregs. It is significant for maintaining immunological homeostasis and avoiding autoimmune disorders. The FOXP3 structural components include a zinc finger domain, a leucine zipper domain, and a forkhead DNA-binding domain, which together enable efficient gene expression control. The leucine zipper domain promotes dimerisation, which is essential for transcriptional activity; at the same time, the forkhead domain, in particular, binds to specific DNA sequences [ 31 ].

sections.section: Importance Of Immune Regulation And Foxp3
sections.text: In addition to defending the body against infections, the immune system works to prevent overreactions that could lead to tissue damage and autoimmune diseases. The immune system’s ability to maintain this balance depends on immune regulation. Autoimmune response dysregulation can lead to a variety of diseases, including cancer, chronic inflammatory conditions, and autoimmune diseases. Tregs are crucial for this control because they express the transcription factor FOXP3. FOXP3 is a master regulator that controls the growth, stability, and function of Tregs. These cells are essential in regulating immune responses and preventing excessive inflammation and autoimmunity by controlling the cytokine environment and preventing other T cells from activating [ 30 , 31 ]. Autoimmunity is prevented by immunological control, which ensures that the immune system does not attack the body’s tissues. Peripheral tolerance, which prevents self-reactive T cells from attacking healthy tissues, is primarily maintained by Tregs. Autoimmune conditions like multiple sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, and type 1 diabetes can develop if the immune system is not adequately controlled. Apart from autoimmunity, immune modulation is crucial in managing chronic inflammation, a defining feature of numerous illnesses such as psoriasis, CRSwNP, and inflammatory bowel disease [ 32 , 33 ]. Tregs resolve inflammation by limiting the production of proinflammatory cytokines and preserving immunological homeostasis through FOXP3 [ 34 ]. FOXP3 is essential for differentiating naive CD4 + T cells into functional Tregs. As seen in Immune Dysregulation, Polyendocrinopathy, Enteropathy, and X-linked Syndrome (IPEX), where patients experience various autoimmune diseases as a result of the lack of functional Tregs, mutations or abnormalities in FOXP3 cause severe immune dysregulation [ 35 ]. By generating anti-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-10 and TGF-β and suppressing the production of proinflammatory cytokines such as IL-6, TNF-α, and IL-17, FOXP3 + Tregs reduce effector T cell responses. This inhibitory function is critical in limiting excessive immunological activation that could damage healthy tissues [ 36 , 37 ]. Additionally, FOXP3 helps stabilise Tregs in inflammatory tissues enabling them to adapt to inflammatory conditions and continue to inhibit [ 38 ]. Many disorders are linked to dysregulation of Treg and FOXP3 function. Reduced or dysfunctional Tregs cause peripheral tolerance mechanisms to fail in autoimmune disorders such as multiple sclerosis and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), allowing self-reactive T cells to assault healthy tissues [ 39 ]. The quantity and functionality of FOXP3 + Tregs are frequently reduced in chronic inflammatory diseases, like inflammatory NPs, which prolong inflammation and damage tissue [ 40 ]. The increased FOXP3 + Tregs in the tumour microenvironment can decrease anti-tumour immunity, enabling tumour cells to elude immune surveillance, even though these cells are crucial for immunological homeostasis in cancer [ 41 ]. Immune modulation and FOXP3 have significant therapeutic potential. One new therapeutic approach for autoimmune illnesses is to increase the quantity or function of Tregs. For instance, IL-2-based therapies, which increase Tregs, are intended to reduce autoimmune symptoms and restore immunological tolerance [ 42 ]. However, in cancer, blocking FOXP3 + Tregs may enhance anti-tumour immunity by enhancing the ability of effector T cells to identify and eliminate cancer cells [ 43 ]. Developing treatments that can alter Treg function for therapeutic benefit requires understanding the processes governing FOXP3 expression and stability [ 44 ].

sections.section: Foxp3 As A Master Transcription Factor Of Tregs
sections.text: FOXP3 is considered the master regulator of Treg cells and is essential for their proper function. Compared to normal T cells, FOXP3 can upregulate or downregulate around half of the genes that are overexpressed or underexpressed in Treg cells [ 45 ]. FOXP3 is produced explicitly by Tregs, and impairment or mutation of FOXP3 cells causes dysregulation in the immune system and leads to autoimmune disorders [ 46 ]. Natural or artificial mutations of the FOXP3 gene cause congenital defects in the production and function of Treg cells. These result in immunological, multi-organ, and spontaneous pathogenesis in immune-dysregulated humans and scurfy mice with X-linked polyendocrinopathy enteropathy (IPEX) syndrome [ 47 – 49 ]. Furthermore, a nearly complete Treg cell-type transcription profile is produced in normal CD4 + T cells with overexpression of FOXP3 and specific transcription factors, including Irf4, Eos, and Gata1 [ 50 ] FOXP3 controls most gene transcription in Treg cells, either alone or in combination with other transcription factors [ 51 , 52 ]. FOXP3 primarily serves as a transcriptional repressor at the molecular level, which helps explain some of the essential traits of Treg cells [ 53 ]. Also, FOXP3 primarily functions as a transcriptional repressor of genes involved in T cell activation and effector processes, such as proinflammatory cytokine production and proliferation. Cytokines, such as interferon (IFN)-γ, IL-2, IL-4, and IL-17 A, simultaneously give the cell strong suppressive capabilities [ 54 , 55 ]. Lineage commitment and stability depend on sustained FOXP3 expression in Treg cells. Several important processes, such as cytokine signalling, epigenetic regulation of the FOXP3 locus, and interactions between FOXP3 and other proteins, help control FOXP3 expression, and in turn, preserve peripheral tolerance.

IL-35 is a heterodimeric cytokine composed of IL-12α and IL-27β chains, primarily produced by Tregs and regulatory B cells (Bregs) [ 56 ]. IL-35 exerts potent immunosuppressive effects by inhibiting T cell proliferation, promoting Treg expansion, and suppressing proinflammatory cytokine production (Fig. 1 ) [ 57 ]. Emerging evidence suggests that dysregulation of IL-35 expression contributes to the pathogenesis of various autoimmune and inflammatory diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis, inflammatory bowel disease, and asthma [ 58 ].

IL-35 is primarily produced by a specialised subset of Tregs known as iTr35 cells. These induced Tregs produce IL-35 in response to inflammatory signals, helping suppress immune responses and maintain immune tolerance [ 59 ].

Bregs can also produce IL-35, particularly in autoimmune or chronic inflammatory environments. IL-35 production by Bregs is often observed in autoimmune diseases and is thought to contribute to their suppressive function [ 60 ].

Specific inflammatory cytokines essentially trigger IL-35 production. IL-27 and TGF-β are among the most significant inducers of IL-35, as they upregulate the expression of the EBI3 and p35 subunits, respectively [ 61 ].

This cytokine increases EBI3 transcription, a critical component of IL-35 production. IL-27 acts on Tregs by binding to its receptor (IL-27R), activating downstream transcriptional factors that lead to EBI3 synthesis [ 62 ].
This cytokine promotes the expression of the p35 subunit. TGF-β signalling activates transcription factors, such as Smad proteins, which increase transcription of the p35 gene [ 63 ].

The production of IL-35 depends on the signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT) proteins, especially STAT1 and STAT3. STAT proteins are activated when IL-27 and TGF-β attach to their respective receptors. These proteins then enter the nucleus to encourage the transcription of the EBI3 and p35 genes [ 64 ]. STAT1: Mainly in charge of upregulating EBI3, STAT1 responds to IL-27 signalling by binding to particular promoter sites on the EBI3 gene [ 65 ]. STAT3: STAT3 is especially significant for Treg-mediated IL-35 production and increases the transcription of both EBI3 and p35 [ 66 ].

The EBI3 and p35 genes contain promoter regions responsive to inflammatory signals, with binding sites for STAT1 and STAT3. The coordination between these two genes is critical for IL-35 formation. Under stimulation, STAT1 binds to the EBI3 promoter, while STAT3 binds to both the EBI3 and p35 promoters. This coordinated transcriptional activation is crucial for producing IL-35 as a functional heterodimer [ 67 ].

sections.section: Protein-Protein Interaction (Ppi) Network: Foxp3-Mediated Regulation Of Il-35 Expression
sections.text: The master transcription factor that defines Tregs, FOXP3, is necessary for the immunosuppressive milieu for which NPs are known. Although FOXP3 does not directly interact with IL-35 at the protein level, it transcriptionally controls the production of the two crucial cytokine subunits, IL-12 A (p35) and EBI3, as shown in Fig. 2 . Key interactions between IL-35 and FOXP3 are explained in Table 1 . Research has shown that FOXP3 Tregs exclusively express IL-35, whereas typical T cells that do not express FOXP3 do not produce it [ 68 ]. It has been demonstrated that IL-35 aids in Treg-mediated suppression by preventing the growth of effector T cells and the generation of inflammatory cytokines [ 69 ]. FOXP3’s promotion of IL-35 expression highlights a transcriptional mechanism in which it serves as a critical node integrating the immunosuppressive cytokine environment and the regulatory T cell lineage [ 70 ]. This mechanism may increase local immunological tolerance in persistent inflammatory conditions, such as nasal polyposis, leading to tissue remodelling and inflammation [ 71 ]. The master transcription factor of regulatory T cells and elements of the IL-35 cytokine complex were built using the STRING database. Individual proteins are represented as nodes, and associations known or expected from co-expression, experimental data, database annotation, and text mining are indicated by edges. FOXP3 may indirectly regulate the IL-35 pathway through its associations with immune-related proteins such as IL12RB2 and IL27RA. The two subunits comprising the IL-35 heterodimer, IL12A and EBI3, are closely related to and common signalling elements like IL12RB2 and IL27. FOXP3 and IL12A/EBI3 do not exhibit a direct PPI, consistent with their transcriptional rather than physical interactions. The network identifies functional similarities between the IL-35 and IL-27 pathways, which could be involved in immune modulation in the pathophysiology of NPs.

sections.section: Tregs And Il-35 Crosstalk In Nasal Polyps
sections.text: The balance between effector and regulatory immune responses is upset in the immunopathogenesis of NPs, especially in eosinophilic CRSwNP. One crucial way Tregs, essential for preserving immunological tolerance, inhibit the immune system is by secreting the potent anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-35. While decreasing Th2-mediated cytokine production, including IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13, which are essential for tissue eosinophilia and polyp formation, IL-35 improves Treg stability and function. Reduced Treg counts or compromised IL-35 signalling lead to mucosal remodelling and persistent inflammation in CRSwNP. A crucial immunoregulatory loop is highlighted by the reciprocal interaction between Tregs and IL-35, in which Tregs generate IL-35, supporting Treg activity. Targeting this Treg–IL-35 axis has the potential to re-establish mucosal immune homeostasis and mitigate polyp growth and recurrence (Table 2 ).

sections.section: Il-35 Is An Immunosuppressive Cytokine With Connections To Foxp3
sections.text: IL-35, a heterodimeric cytokine composed of the Epstein-Barr virus-induced gene 3 (EBI3) and the IL-12α subunit, plays a significant role in immune regulation. Under certain circumstances, Tregs and other immune cells are the primary sources of this immunosuppressive cytokine [ 61 ]. By preventing the growth of effector T cells such as Th17 and Th1 cells and promoting the development of induced Tregs, IL-35 helps maintain immunological tolerance. By activating the STAT1 and STAT4 signalling pathways, this cytokine suppresses inflammation and maintains immunological homeostasis by modifying the immune system [ 76 ]. The immunosuppressive properties of IL-35 make it a potential therapeutic target in autoimmune diseases and transplant rejection. A crucial interaction with FOXP3, the master transcription factor of Tregs, highlights the immunosuppressive potential of IL-35. The growth, stability, and functionality of naturally occurring and induced Tregs depend on FOXP3. It has been shown that IL-35 increases FOXP3 expression, thereby strengthening Treg-mediated immune suppression [ 57 ]. On the other hand, FOXP3 expression promotes IL-35 secretion by Tregs, creating a feedback loop that reinforces immunological tolerance. Its therapeutic potential in immunological disorders is highlighted by the complex interaction between IL-35 and FOXP3, which is essential for maintaining immune homeostasis and against autoimmune reactions [ 76 ].

sections.section: Foxp3, Il-35, And The Microenvironment Of Inflammatory Polyps
sections.text: Tregs are the primary cell type that suppresses immunopathological responses in the host immune system to antigens [ 77 ]. Furthermore, extensive research has highlighted the involvement of Tregs in the pathogenesis and therapeutic strategies for various inflammatory conditions, including autoimmune diseases, cancers, allergies, transplantation, and tissue engineering [ 78 ]. However, screening Tregs is crucial for monitoring immune balance, diagnosing diseases, and optimising therapeutic strategies. Tregs are identified by key markers that define their phenotype and function. The transcription factor FOXP3 is the most specific marker, while CD25 (IL-2Rα) is highly expressed and crucial for their survival. Low CD127 (IL-7Rα) expression helps distinguish Tregs from conventional T cells. Functional markers such as CTLA-4, GITR, CD39, CD73, LAG-3, and TIGIT contribute to their immunosuppressive role. Helios is often used to differentiate thymic-derived Tregs from peripherally induced ones. Migration markers like CCR4, CCR7, and CD62L also help track Treg trafficking to specific tissues. These markers, often combined, enable accurate identification and functional assessment of Tregs in research and clinical applications [ 79 ]. FOXP3 is the primary regulator of Treg formation and is, in fact, essential for their differentiation and suppressive function. Additionally, FOXP3 + Tregs have been identified throughout the body, exhibit immunosuppressive properties, and use a variety of mechanisms to reduce unnecessary inflammatory responses when exposed to self-antigens and foreign antigens [ 78 ]. In mice, Treg-mediated T cell suppression is enhanced when TCF-1 expression is reduced in Tregs. TCF-1 typically functions as a suppressor of genes co-bound by FOXP3. Consequently, this enhanced suppression promotes tumour growth in polyposis, underscoring the importance of Treg TCF-1 expression for sufficient tumour clearance [ 79 ]. Similarly, inflammatory diseases like NPs have been linked to the regulation of FOXP3 + Tregs. Research has revealed that NP downregulates FOXP3 + Tregs, which may contribute to chronic inflammation. It is worth noting that intranasal steroid therapy has been shown to increase Treg numbers and activity, resulting in an anti-inflammatory effect via a recently discovered mechanism. These results reveal that NP and other chronic inflammatory disorders, such as tumour-associated polyposis, might benefit from a therapy targeting Tregs [ 80 ]. Immunological repression and increased Treg activity depend on the cytokine IL-35. It stabilises Tregs, promotes their growth, and activates a particular subgroup of Tregs that produce IL-35 (iTR35 cells) [ 74 ]. By improving the stability and suppressive capabilities of FOXP3 + Tregs, IL-35 strengthens immunological tolerance and lowers excessive inflammation [ 81 ]. Interestingly, IL-35 can activate a unique subgroup of Tregs called iTR35 cells, which mediate suppression independently of FOXP3 but dependent on IL-35. Increased IL-35 levels can aid Treg-mediated inhibition of effector T cells, promoting tumour growth and immune evasion in tumour polyposis [ 70 ]. On the other hand, decreased IL-35 expression has been linked to an immunological regulatory imbalance in NP and other inflammatory nasal diseases, leading to tissue remodelling and ongoing inflammation (Fig. 3 ). Remarkably, intranasal steroid treatment may increase IL-35 production and restore Treg function in NP, intensifying its immunosuppressive effects. These findings suggest modulating IL-35 levels could be a promising strategy for controlling immune responses in cancer-related polyposis and NP. Future research should explore IL-35-based therapies to restore immune balance, prevent disease progression, and improve treatment outcomes in patients suffering from chronic inflammatory diseases.

sections.section: Pharmacotherapeutic Modulation Of Immune Dysregulation In Crswnp
sections.text: CRSwNP is a persistent inflammatory condition characterised by a type 2 immune response, involving elevated levels of IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, and immunoglobulin E (IgE), along with eosinophilic infiltration. This immune profile is commonly characterised by reduced regulatory T cell (Treg) activity and diminished FOXP3 expression, the key transcription factor governing Treg development and functional stability. Current pharmacologic interventions aim to suppress type 2-driven inflammatory responses and restore immune homeostasis by enhancing Treg-mediated immunoregulation [ 80 ]. Corticosteroids, administered intranasally or systemically, remain the mainstay of treating CRSwNP, as explained in Fig. 4 . These agents suppress type 2 inflammatory mediators, particularly IL-5 and IL-13, thereby reducing eosinophil survival and mucosal oedema. Beyond their anti-inflammatory properties, corticosteroids may enhance regulatory T cell (Treg) function by modulating the local cytokine milieu. Studies have demonstrated that corticosteroid exposure can upregulate FOXP3 mRNA expression in nasal tissues, suggesting a potential role in Treg induction. However, this immunomodulatory effect is variable and patient-dependent. Long-term systemic corticosteroid use is additionally constrained by adverse effects and rebound inflammation following discontinuation. Thus, while corticosteroids offer symptomatic relief and partial immune rebalancing, their limitations highlight the need for alternative or adjunctive therapies, as shown in [ 81 ]. Biologic therapies have emerged as targeted and potentially disease-modifying interventions for CRSwNP, particularly in patients with type 2 inflammation. Dupilumab, a monoclonal antibody against the IL-4 receptor alpha IL-4Rα, inhibits both IL-4 and IL-13 signalling pathways, attenuating eosinophilic recruitment, mucus hypersecretion, and epithelial barrier dysfunction. Importantly, dupilumab has demonstrated the capacity to restore FOXP3⁺ regulatory T cell (Treg) populations within nasal polyp tissue, suggesting enhanced immunoregulatory activity [ 82 ]. Clinically, dupilumab is associated with significant reductions in polyp size and improvements in olfactory function. Mepolizumab, an anti-IL-5 monoclonal antibody, effectively reduces circulating and tissue eosinophil counts and mitigates exacerbation rates in eosinophilic airway disease. However, its influence on Treg activity and FOXP3 expression appears minimal, indicating a predominantly anti-inflammatory mechanism rather than direct immunomodulation [ 83 ]. Omalizumab, targeting immunoglobulin E (IgE), reduces mast cell activation and downstream cytokine release. While its impact on Treg function is variable, some studies report modest increases in FOXP3 expression and restoration of Treg-inducing capacity in plasmacytoid dendritic cells [ 84 ]. Dupilumab exhibits the most comprehensive modulation of inflammatory cytokines and immunoregulatory pathways among these agents. Stapokibart (CM310) (Kangyueda ® ) is an IgG4 monoclonal antibody that specifically targets IL-4Rα [ 85 ]. KeyMed Biosciences is developing it and was approved in China in December 2024 for the treatment of chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (CRSwNP) [ 86 ]. The binding of stapokibart to IL-4Rα inhibits the binding and subsequent signalling of IL-4 and IL-13, type 2 cytokines that are pivotal in inflammation [ 87 , 88 ]. Type 2 cytokines and chemokines that attract eosinophils to the nasal mucosa are generated by both immune and stromal cells, with IL-4Rα being extensively expressed and efficiently inhibited by anti-IL-4Rα monoclonal antibodies [ 89 ]. Thus, the nasal polyps, dominated by type 2 inflammation treated with a daily intranasal corticosteroid, stapokibart, showed a reduction in polyp size and severity of nasal symptoms at 24 weeks [ 86 ]. Macrolides, especially clarithromycin, have attracted interest for their anti-inflammatory effects that extend beyond their antimicrobial properties. They appear to reduce proinflammatory mediators such as IL-8 and tumour necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α). They may support Treg function in patients with non-type 2 or mixed endotype CRSwNP. However, their overall immunomodulatory impact is relatively modest, and current evidence linking macrolide therapy to meaningful FOXP3 upregulation remains limited and inconsistent [ 90 ]. Leukotriene receptor antagonists like montelukast act by dampening leukotriene D4-driven inflammation, improving symptom control. However, their role in modulating regulatory immune responses is minimal. So far, there is little convincing evidence that they directly influence Treg induction or FOXP3 expression. Similarly, aspirin desensitisation has been shown to be beneficial in aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD) by reshaping arachidonic acid metabolism and reducing disease severity. However, the extent to which this intervention affects Treg activity or restores FOXP3 expression remains poorly defined [ 91 ]. These therapies offer varying degrees of anti-inflammatory benefit, but their ability to restore immune balance by promoting Tregs and FOXP3 remains uncertain. Among all pharmacological options, biologics—particularly dupilumab—stand out for their more comprehensive immunomodulatory profile. Dupilumab suppresses key type 2 cytokines and enhances Treg activity and FOXP3 expression, suggesting a capacity to re-establish immune tolerance. Corticosteroids continue to serve as a mainstay in treatment, though their effects on regulatory pathways are less consistent and tend to diminish after cessation. Looking ahead, the most effective pharmacotherapies for CRSwNP will likely be those that control inflammation and support the regeneration of immune regulation, particularly through the expansion and functional stability of FOXP3 + Tregs.

sections.section: Key Biomarkers, Cytokine Mediators, And Emerging Therapies In Type 2 Inflammatory Airway Diseases
sections.text: Prominent biomarkers for type 2 inflammatory airway diseases include fractional exhaled nitric oxide (FeNO), thymus and activation-regulated chemokine (TARC), eotaxin, periostin, IgE, and blood eosinophil counts (Table 3 ). These biomarkers can improve disease targeting, enhance patients’ health-related quality of life, and lower the long-term direct and indirect financial burdens associated with inadequate asthma management. Cytokine mediators produce FeNO and blood eosinophil count [ 92 – 96 ].

sections.section: Therapeutic Implications Of Targeting Il-35 And Foxp3
sections.text: In the meantime, TGF-β plays a role in fibrosis and tissue remodelling, which are characteristics of chronic inflammation in NPs [ 104 ]. Pseudocyst formation, basement membrane thickening, and glandular hyperplasia are examples of structural alterations induced by chronic inflammation that prolong blockage and cause additional inflammation [ 105 ]. Another significant element in the development of NP is microbial dysbiosis. By generating superantigens and inducing an excessive immune response, an imbalance in the nasal microbiota, especially when Staphylococcus aureus is dominant, aggravates inflammation [ 106 ]. Regulatory immune pathways also play a crucial role in modulating NP inflammation. IL-35, an immunosuppressive cytokine primarily produced by Tregs, has inhibited excessive inflammatory responses by suppressing Th2 and Th17 cell activity [ 107 ]. Similarly, FOXP3, a key transcription factor in Tregs, is essential for maintaining immune tolerance and limiting chronic inflammation in NPs [ 108 ]. Dysregulation of IL-35 and FOXP3 can contribute to persistent inflammation and polyp growth. Targeted treatments have been developed due to an understanding of the immunological underpinnings of NPs. By altering specific immune pathways, biologic drugs such as anti-IL-5 (e.g., mepolizumab), anti-IL-4/IL-13 (e.g., dupilumab), and anti-IgE (e.g., omalizumab) have demonstrated efficacy in reducing polyp size and alleviating symptoms [ 107 ]. Emerging therapeutic strategies aimed at enhancing IL-35 signalling or promoting FOXP3 + Treg function may offer additional benefits in restoring immune balance and preventing polyp recurrence [ 109 ]. These developments highlight the importance of analysing the immune systems underlying NPs to create individualised treatment plans.

This review has several limitations that should be considered. It is a narrative review and did not use a formal systematic search strategy or a meta-analysis approach. This may have reduced both its comprehensiveness and reproducibility. The current evidence on FOXP3 and IL-35 in nasal polyps remains limited, and studies vary widely in design, sample size, patient characteristics, and experimental methods, making direct comparisons across the literature difficult. In addition, most available data come from preclinical models and observational clinical studies. As a result, the causal relationships between impaired immunoregulation and nasal polyp development remain poorly established. Any proposed therapeutic relevance of FOXP3 or IL-35 should therefore be interpreted with caution, especially given the lack of strong clinical trial evidence. Several confounding factors may also have influenced the findings, including demographic differences, comorbid conditions, inflammatory endotypes, and prior treatments. Overall, these limitations point to the need for more rigorous translational research and better-designed clinical studies to further clarify and strengthen the current evidence base.

Targeting immunoregulatory molecules such as IL-35 and FOXP3 may help treat type 2 inflammatory airway diseases, including CRSwNP. IL-35 decreases Th2-mediated inflammation by inhibiting key cytokines such as IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13; its deficiency has been observed in severe, steroid-resistant instances. Similarly, maintaining immunological tolerance depends on FOXP3, the regulator of regulatory T cells. Impaired FOXP3 expression leads to polyp formation and prolonged eosinophilic inflammation. Enhancing FOXP3 and IL-35 activity may improve immunological balance, reduce tissue remodelling, and improve long-term disease control, making them desirable targets for further immunotherapeutic approaches in CRSwNP.
